key_insight: Pretrained protein language models (pLMs) can introduce hidden data leakage into protein–protein interaction (PPI) inference pipelines, causing inflated performance scores. Standard evaluation protocols can therefore overestimate model accuracy when pLM-derived embeddings are used.
problem_solved: Identifies and demonstrates the source of misleadingly high PPI prediction performance caused by information leakage from pretrained pLMs, and highlights the need for leakage-aware evaluation and benchmarking.
method: Analyze PPI inference workflows that use pretrained pLM embeddings to identify potential pathways for information leakage between pretraining, training, and test sets.
Run controlled experiments comparing models with/without pLM embeddings and with stricter data-splitting strategies to quantify the effect of leakage on reported performance.
Recommend evaluation checks and protocol adjustments (e.g., stricter homology or sequence-similarity splits, baselines) to isolate genuine predictive signal from leaked information.
impact: Alerts ML practitioners and benchmarkers that using pLM embeddings without leakage controls can produce overoptimistic results, prompting revised evaluation standards for reliable PPI model comparison and deployment.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing flow from pLM pretraining → embedding extraction → PPI model training, with arrows highlighting where leakage can occur
Bar chart comparing PPI accuracy/AUPR with standard evaluation vs. leakage-controlled evaluation (showing performance drop)
Schematic of data-splitting strategies (random split vs. homology-aware split) to illustrate safe evaluation practices
Checklist infographic of recommended mitigations (e.g., stricter splits, negative controls, reporting of embedding sources)
paper_title: A flaw in using pretrained protein language models in protein–protein interaction inference models
